title: The Inverse Polynomial over a Commutative Ring
content: The definition that carries the whole entry: $\mathrm{invPoly}\ A := C(\mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0))\cdot \mathrm{div}_X(\mathrm{charpoly}\ A)$, where $c_0 = (\mathrm{charpoly}\ A).\mathrm{coeff}\ 0$. The only change from the field-case parent is that the field inverse $(-c_0)^{-1}$ is replaced by $\mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0)$, which agrees with the field inverse on units and returns $0$ on non-units. Everything downstream shows that evaluating this explicit polynomial at $A$ returns $A^{-1}$ whenever $\det A$ is a unit. It is `noncomputable` only because it references the classically-defined `charpoly`; it is a concrete element of $R[X]$ once the characteristic polynomial is known.
mathContext: $r = C(\mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0))\cdot \mathrm{div}_X p$ with $p = \mathrm{charpoly}\ A$; $\deg r < \deg p = n$ and $(\mathrm{aeval}\ A)\ r = A^{-1}$.

title: A Unit Determinant Forces a Unit Constant Term
content: The single place invertibility enters, and the only genuinely new argument over the field parent. By `Matrix.det_eq_sign_charpoly_coeff`, $\det A = (-1)^n c_0$. Since $(-1)^n$ is its own inverse ($((-1)^n)^2 = 1$), we can solve $c_0 = (-1)^n \det A$, a product of the unit $(-1)^n$ and the unit $\det A$; hence $c_0$ is a unit, and therefore so is $-c_0$. Over a field this collapses to the parent's statement '$\det A \neq 0 \Rightarrow c_0 \neq 0$', but the unit formulation is exactly what is needed to invert $-c_0$ via `Ring.inverse` over a general commutative ring.
mathContext: Over a commutative ring a square matrix is invertible iff $\det A$ is a unit — strictly stronger than $\det A \neq 0$ (e.g. $\det = 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}$). The identity $c_0 = (-1)^n \det A$ transfers that unit to the constant term.

title: Cayley–Hamilton in Additive Form
content: The engine, valid over any commutative ring. Cayley–Hamilton (`Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly`) gives $(\mathrm{aeval}\ A)(\mathrm{charpoly}\ A) = 0$. Rewriting $\mathrm{charpoly}\ A = \mathrm{div}_X(\mathrm{charpoly}\ A)\cdot X + C\,c_0$ (`Polynomial.divX_mul_X_add`) and pushing `aeval` through the sum and product turns this into $(\mathrm{div}_X p)(A)\cdot A + c_0\bullet 1 = 0$. This isolates the relation '(a polynomial in $A$) times $A$ equals a scalar', which is precisely what an inverse formula needs.
mathContext: $(\mathrm{div}_X p)(A)\cdot A = -c_0 \bullet 1$; the constant term $c_0$ becomes the scalar obstruction that a unit determinant lets us invert.

title: Dividing by the Unit −c₀ to Exhibit A⁻¹
content: The heart of the inversion. From $(\mathrm{div}_X p)(A)\cdot A = -c_0\bullet 1$ and $(\mathrm{aeval}\ A)(\mathrm{invPoly}\ A) = \mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0)\bullet(\mathrm{div}_X p)(A)$, one computes $(\mathrm{aeval}\ A)(\mathrm{invPoly}\ A)\cdot A = \mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0)\bullet(-c_0\bullet 1) = (\mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0)\cdot(-c_0))\bullet 1 = 1$, where the last step is `Ring.inverse_mul_cancel` applied to the unit $-c_0$ — the exact replacement for the field division $(-c_0)^{-1}(-c_0)=1$. `Matrix.inv_eq_left_inv` then promotes this left inverse to the genuine nonsingular inverse: $A^{-1} = (\mathrm{aeval}\ A)(\mathrm{invPoly}\ A)$.
mathContext: $A^{-1} = \mathrm{Ring.inverse}(-c_0)\bullet(\mathrm{div}_X p)(A) = (\mathrm{aeval}\ A)(\mathrm{invPoly}\ A)$, the main theorem over a commutative ring.

title: Degree Bound and Membership in R[A]
content: Two structural corollaries. `invPoly_natDegree_lt`: since $\mathrm{invPoly}\ A = C(\ldots)\cdot \mathrm{div}_X p$, its degree is at most $\deg(\mathrm{div}_X p) < \deg p = \mathrm{Fintype.card}\ n$ (using `natDegree_C_mul_le`, `degree_divX_lt`, and `charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim`, which needs `Nontrivial R`). `inv_mem_adjoin`: because $A^{-1}$ is $\mathrm{aeval}\ A$ of a polynomial, it lies in $\mathrm{Algebra.adjoin}\ R\ \{A\} = R[A]$ via `Algebra.adjoin_singleton_eq_range_aeval`.
mathContext: $\deg(\mathrm{invPoly}\ A) < n$ and $A^{-1} \in R[A]$: the inverse is a low-degree polynomial in $A$ lying inside the commutative subalgebra generated by $A$.
relatedConcepts: Algebra.adjoin as the range of aeval

title: Reconciliation with the Adjugate and the GL(n, ℤ) Witness
content: Two closing points that pin down the generality. `inv_eq_smul_adjugate` records that the polynomial inverse computed here is literally the same matrix as Mathlib's adjugate-based nonsingular inverse $A^{-1} = \mathrm{Ring.inverse}(\det A)\bullet \mathrm{adjugate}\ A$ (`Matrix.inv_def`) — two descriptions of one object, no hypothesis needed. The final `example` over $\mathbb{Z}$ makes the upgrade concrete: any integer matrix with $\det = \pm 1$ (the group $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$) has its inverse inside the integer-coefficient subalgebra $\mathbb{Z}[A]$ — a statement the field-only parent cannot even phrase, since $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a field.
mathContext: $A^{-1} = \mathrm{Ring.inverse}(\det A)\bullet\mathrm{adjugate}\ A$; over $\mathbb{Z}$ with $\det A$ a unit, $A^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}[A]$.
